JALANDHAR The first of the four names with a sword hanging over their heads called it a day on Tuesday. Nine years after he first donned the Indian jersey, 31-year-old Nilakanta Sharma declared that the ongoing Asian Champions Trophy (ACT) would be his last. A member of the gold-winning 2016 Junior World Cup side and one of the nearly dozen players to make a successful transition to the senior squad, Nilakanta was also part of the Indian team that won Olympic bronze in Tokyo. One final chapter. Let’s give him the farewell he deserves. 🥹🇮🇳 #HockeyIsBack #HACT2026 #SatSriAkalAsia #IndiaKaGame— Hockey India (@TheHockeyIndia) October 27, 2026 “My retirement decision was actually taken after the first game at the Nagoya Asian Games. I slept over it through the night and thought about it, talked to my family and the coach also. As a senior player, many times when you play day in and day out for so many years, there is sometimes a thought of moving on. I thought I had played a lot, I had an Olympic medal and it was time to let others get a chance,” a visibly emotional Nilakanta told Sportstar after India’s opening match here. “I am actually very satisfied with the decision. I am getting a chance to go out on the ground, which is the biggest thing a player can ask for. I have seen a lot of players, big names, legends even, who keep playing and continue to drag and then one fine day, suddenly, they are out, discarded. That is never a good feeling and I didn’t want that for myself,” he insisted. While explaining his talk with coach Craig Fulton, Nilakanta also admitted that his career would have perhaps been over earlier if India had failed to defend its Asian Games gold earlier this month. “I told the coach to give me a chance to say goodbye after the ACT in Punjab. He agreed on the condition that we won gold in Nagoya and qualify for LA Olympics. If we had not got gold there, I don’t think I would have been playing here at all,” he said. While he is yet to decide on a future course of action, coaching is definitely on the midfielder’s radar. “Maybe, after a few months and depending on how things pan out. Whenever I go back home, I coach the youngsters in Manipur. I specifically chose sports department when the Manipur government offered me a job after Tokyo so that whatever I have learnt over the years from all my coaches, including Graham Reid and Fulton, I can pass it on to the juniors, share my experiences and create new players,” he declared.
